name: Faroese
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand sources agree (2 agree, 1 refine), none contradicts
catalog_quote: 14.1. Stress. The general rule in Faroese is that stress is on the first syllable. The stressed vowels are underlined: renna 'to run', avtala 'to arrange', 'arrangement', and so on. Borrowings from Danish have the same stress pattern as in Danish (or sometimes in English)
sweep_summary: Faroese (faro1244) is in the catalog as fixed-strict (initial), deciding source Petersen & Adams 2009 §14.1 p. 275 (a pedagogical grammar, verified in the earlier reading). The single works with stress in the title, Árnason 1999 'Word stress in Modern Icelandic and Faroese' (pp. 567-586 inside ch. 8 of van der Hulst ed., Eurotyp 20-4; DOI 10.1515/9783110197082.2.477), is relevant but unobtainable: De Gruyter WAF-blocked, no Google Books/HathiTrust/archive.org/Open Library copy; only secondhand content (Dehé & Wetterlin 2013: 231 and Harbert 2007: 81) which agrees with initial stress plus non-initial compound adverbs and loans. New in this search of works with stress in the title: an open archive.org (Google Books full-view) scan of Young & Clewer 1985 reproduces Lockwood's 1964 grammar pronunciation chapter verbatim, whose 'Stress' section (p. 10) states initial stress in nearly all native words, secondary stress on the second compound member, systematic exceptions in 3+-syllable ó-/sam- words and non-initial stress in loanwords — a first-hand descriptive-grammar statement that confirms the classification and refines the exception set; proposed as the new deciding source (or as co-source with the 2009 grammar). Dehé & Wetterlin 2013 (already held) re-read: confirms, quoting Thráinsson et al. 2004: 28. Harbert 2007 (secondary) confirms. Still unheld and high priority: Árnason 1999 (De Gruyter), Árnason 2011 OUP ch. 13, Thráinsson et al. 2004/2012 p. 28 (print only), Petersen & Voeltzel 2025 De Gruyter ch. 6. Bing/DDG by automated download returned nothing usable

new_statements.quote: The stres[s] falls on the first syllable in nearly all native Faroese words; the second element in compounds carries subsidiary stress. ... Exceptions are words of three or more syllables containing the prefixes ó- or sam-, when the stress may also fall on the second syllable: ótespiligur ... unpleasant, sambærligur ... agreeable; notice also marghátligur ... peculiar, upptalcoyti ... addition, addendum. The prefix al- (lit. all) is unstressed in aloftast ... most frequently. Words of foreign origin often bear the stress on syllables other than the first, e.g.: lærarinna (female) teacher, studentur student, forargiligur annoying, vexing, forbanna to curse.

new_statements.reading: First-hand descriptive statement by the author of the Glottolog-listed reference grammar (Lockwood 1955/1964/1977): primary stress on the first syllable in nearly all native words, secondary stress on the second member of compounds; the only systematic native exceptions are 3+-syllable words with the prefixes ó-/sam- (variable initial or second-syllable stress) plus a few listed lexical items; loanwords often carry non-initial stress. This is the same coding as the catalog (fixed initial, word domain, loan caveat) and it agrees with the reference-grammar rule quoted by Dehé & Wetterlin 2013 ('Primary stress falls on the first syllable in all native Faroese words', Thráinsson et al. 2004: 28) and with the secondhand reports of Árnason 1999 (initial stress; non-initial in some compound adverbs and loans). It refines 'fixed-strict' by naming the native prefix exceptions; a reclassify is not warranted on the catalog's own precedent (Icelandic, Polish kept fixed-strict with comparable exceptions). Caveat: 1964 description, read through the 1985 verbatim reproduction (scanned text; 'stresd' = 'stress'); the transcriptions in the scanned are garbled and were omitted from the quote.

sources.quote: Word stress in the modern GMC languages is treated in detail in Zonneveld et al. 1999. Among these languages, only Insular Scandinavian (IC and FA) has remained true to the GMC preference for initial stress, and these languages have apparently even strengthened it, since prefixes are generally stressed in them. Lockwood notes that there are few exceptions in FA, of a systematic nature only in cases of words with three or more syllables which begin with the prefixes ó- 'un' or sam- 'together', for example, sambærligur 'agreeable' which is variably accented on the first or second syllable. Non-initial accent is making some inroads through borrowing, however, as in studentur 'student'.
sources.note: Secondary survey: Faroese (with Icelandic) keeps Germanic initial stress, prefixes generally stressed; exceptions per Lockwood (ó-/sam- words of 3+ syllables) and loanwords. Not first-hand; repeats Lockwood and Zonneveld et al. 1999.
